title_en: Application: A formula for the inverse of a matrix

t.en: Find the cofactor matrix and the adjugate of a matrix.
Find the inverse of a matrix using the adjugate formula.

The determinant of a matrix also provides a way to find the inverse of a matrix. Recall the definition of the inverse of a matrix from Definition “The inverse of a matrix”. If $A$ is an $n\times n$-matrix, we say that $A^{-1}$ is the inverse of $A$ if $AA^{-1} = I$ and $A^{-1}A=I$.
We now define a new matrix called the **cofactor matrix** of $A$. The cofactor matrix of $A$ is the matrix whose $\ijth$ entry is the $\ijth$ cofactor of $A$.
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$-matrix. Then the \textbfcofactor matrix of $A$, denoted $\cof(A)$, is defined by

blocks.tex:
\cof(A)
    ~=~ \mat{C_{ij}}
    ~=~ \left[\begin{array}{cccc}
      C_{11} & C_{12} & \cdots & C_{1n} \\
      C_{21} & C_{22} & \cdots & C_{2n} \\
      \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
      C_{n1} & C_{n2} & \cdots & C_{nn} \\
    \end{array}\right],

t.en: where $C_{ij}$ is the $\ijth$ cofactor of $A$.

It is always a good idea to double-check your work. At the end of the calculation, it is very easy to compute $A^{-1}A$ and check whether it is equal to $I$. If they are not equal, be sure to go back and double-check each step. One common mistake is to forget to take the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so be sure not to forget this step.

In practice, it is usually much faster to compute the inverse by the method of Section 〔引用〕, because this only requires solving a single system of equations, rather than computing a large number of cofactors. However, there are some situations where the adjugate formula is useful. One such situation is when the matrix has complicated entries that are functions rather than numbers. The following example illustrates this.
Let

blocks.tex:
A(t) =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      e^{t} & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & \cos t & \sin t \\
      0 & -\sin t & \cos t
    \end{array}\right].

t.en: Show that $A(t)^{-1}$ exists and find it.
First note that
Therefore $A(t)^{-1}$ exists for all values of the variable $t$. The cofactor matrix is

blocks.tex:
\cof(A(t))
    ~=~ \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      1 & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & e^{t}\cos t & e^{t}\sin t \\
      0 & -e^{t}\sin t & e^{t}\cos t
    \end{array}\right].

t.en: The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, and therefore the inverse is

blocks.tex:
A(t)^{-1}
    ~=~ \frac{1}{\det(A(t))}\adj(A(t))
    ~=~
    \frac{1}{e^{t}}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      1 & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & e^{t}\cos t & -e^{t}\sin t \\
      0 & e^{t}\sin t & e^{t}\cos t
    \end{array}\right]
    ~=~ \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      e^{-t} & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & \cos t & -\sin t \\
      0 & \sin t & \cos t
    \end{array}\right].

Does there exist a value of $t$ for which this matrix fails to be invertible? Explain.

Does there exist a value of $t$ for which this matrix fails to be invertible? Explain.
$\det(A) = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & t & t^2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2t \\ t & 0 & 2 \end{array}\right| = t^3+2$, and so $A$ has no inverse when $t=-\sqrt[3]{2}$.

t.en: Consider the matrix

stem.tex:
A =
    \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      e^{t} & \cosh t & \sinh t \\
      e^{t} & \sinh t & \cosh t \\
      e^{t} & \cosh t & \sinh t
    \end{array}\right].

t.en: Does there exist a value of $t$ for which this matrix fails to be invertible? Explain.
Since the matrix $A$ has two identical rows, we have $\det(A)=0$ for all $t$. So this matrix is non-invertible for all $t$.

t.en: Consider the matrix

stem.tex:
A =
    \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      e^{t} & e^{-t}\cos t & e^{-t}\sin t \\
      e^{t} & -e^{-t}\cos t-e^{-t}\sin t & -e^{-t}\sin t+e^{-t}\cos t \\
      e^{t} & 2e^{-t}\sin t & -2e^{-t}\cos t
    \end{array}\right].

t.en: Does there exist a value of $t$ for which this matrix fails to be invertible? Explain.

sol.tex:
\det \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
        e^{t} & e^{-t}\cos t & e^{-t}\sin t \\
        e^{t} & -e^{-t}\cos t-e^{-t}\sin t & -e^{-t}\sin t+e^{-t}\cos t \\
        e^{t} & 2e^{-t}\sin t & -2e^{-t}\cos t
      \end{array}\right] = 5e^{-t} \neq 0

t.en: and so this matrix is always invertible.

t.en: Use the adjugate formula to find the inverse of the matrix

stem.tex:
A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
      e^{t} & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & \cos t & \sin t \\
      0 & \cos t-\sin t & \cos t+\sin t
    \end{array}\right].

sol.tex:
\det \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
        e^{t} & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & \cos t & \sin t \\
        0 & \cos t-\sin t & \cos t+\sin t
      \end{array}\right] = e^{t}.

t.en: Hence the inverse is

sol.tex:
e^{-t}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & e^{t}\cos t+e^{t}\sin t & -e^t(\cos t-\sin t) \\
        0 & -e^{t}\sin t & e^{t}\cos t
      \end{array}\right]^T \\
      ~=~ \left[\begin{array}{ccc}
        e^{-t} & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & \cos t+\sin t  & -\sin t \\
        0 & \sin t-\cos t  & \cos t
      \end{array}\right].
